https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cme3.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Trump met with top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday to discuss AI Published 37 minutes ago US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age". The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry. The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI and a slowdown in developing the technology, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity. Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House. 1. AI 'self-regulation' pact Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside House Speaker Mike Johnson and top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting. The president told reporters that the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks. Under the agreement, which Trump posted on social media, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology. The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues, the document said. They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways." The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. "It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said, referring to the agreement. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president." Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, Trump with top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board. The president has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks, dismissing them as a "hoax". He has said the only "guardrails" the industry needs is a "smart" president. OpenAI and Anthropic have in recent weeks called for tighter oversight of the industry and foe a slowdown of development of the technology. On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model , GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns. The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after several high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation . 2. Doubling down on data centres Trump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI. The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the country over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on from communities. Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November. A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News , external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas. Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres. "These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters. Trump previously said on social media that the only reason communities in the US should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor". "The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame," he said. Huang from Nvidia, which produces computer chips essential for running AI, said after the meeting that data centres should be called "super intelligence factories". These facilities are "reindustrialising the United States", creating jobs across the economy, he added. 3. It's now 'Super Intelligence' Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of term artificial intelligence. SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, and other non-statutory documents within the executive branch," the order said. "As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said. During an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake". Some tech leaders and other people close to the president have already started to use the term. Zuckerberg said on social media on Monday: "We believe superintelligence will create significant new opportunities for all people and businesses." On Wednesday, Musk reposted a clip of tech executives gathered around Trump at the White House, with the words: "Super Intelligence." But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction in the industry because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems. Built on the CORE One platform, the INDX produces flawless and nearly waste-free multicolor and multimaterial prints at record speed. $2,249 at Prusa Check Amazon Check Best Buy Reasons to buy + Very little waste + Core XY speed + Perfect first layer + Very quiet + Fully assembled or DIY kit + Can run completely offline Reasons to avoid - Expensive - No profile for Flex at launch Best picks for you Best Multicolor 3D Printers of 2026: Print the Rainbow The Best 3D Printers for Home, Workshop or Business in 2026 Best Budget 3D Printers 2026 Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test . The Prusa INDX is a revolutionary new toolchanger capable of printing up to eight colors of various materials. INDX stands for In duction D ynamic E x truder, with each slim toolhead having no moving parts, just a nozzle and filament path. The extruder, or “smart head,” does all the work. INDX is a collaborative project between Prusa Research and Bondtech. Prusa makes the platform, in this case a CORE One+ Gen 2 , while Bondtech produces the toolhead system. The two companies have a long history of working together, going back to 2017’s MK3 bedslinger. The INDX can also be purchased separately on Bondtech’s site as a DIY kit to be mounted on any open-source 3D printer you feel like modding. There are definite advantages of going with the Prusa INDX. You can buy it ready to roll, premounted on CORE One that’s ready to print ten minutes after removing it from the box. Even purchasing it as a kit from Prusa removes a lot of hassle and headache, as the kit is custom-fitted to CORE One, with all the wiring, programming, and whatnot done for you. Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware Watch full video here: Sorting through the website to figure out what combination of kit and printer you need is the hardest part of the INDX experience. If you already have a CORE One, prices start at $749 for a four-color INDX “conversion” kit. Prusa optimistically says the kit takes 5 to 6 hours to install, but it took me the better part of a weekend to disassemble my machine and rebuild it as an INDX when I tested out the early Founder’s Edition . The Prusa INDX is the first multicolor 3D printer to ditch the prime tower, making it practically waste-free. While all toolchangers can seriously cut down on wasted material by virtue of having a nozzle for each color, they still need to “prime” the nozzles before printing. This priming creates a tower of wasted material. Prusa has circumvented the prime tower with a new wiper mechanism that quickly shoots out a tiny blob of filament that’s about 13 milligrams in size – smaller than a grain of rice. In my testing, I found the Prusa INDX was faster and less wasteful than any other toolchanger in the workshop. I ran the same model with similar settings on both the Prusa INDX and the Bambu Lab H2C, the closest machine to a toolchanger that Bambu currently has in production. The INDX was able to run it nearly nine hours faster, with 83.58 grams less wasted material (not counting supports) and 3 more colors. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Prusa CORE One+ INDX 8-Tool at Prusa for $2,249 The CORE One+ INDX starts at $1,699 for a DIY kit with four toolheads and goes up to $2,119 for an assembled 3D printer with eight toolheads, plus a Buddy Cam and Advanced filtration. If you already have the printer, the conversion kit is $749 for four toolheads and $999 for eight. There is no pricing for individual toolheads at the moment, but you can start with four toolheads and later add more. Individual tools are currently $45 on the Bondtech website. $2,249 View No price information Check Amazon No price information Check Best Buy We check over 250 million products every day for the best prices Prusa CORE One+ INDX: Included in the Box (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The Prusa CORE One+ INDX we received was pre-assembled and included eight toolheads. It only needed to be unpacked, have its screen mounted, then snap on the spool holders and Bowden tubes. Besides tools, the printer comes with a full spool of Galaxy Black Prusament PLA, a USB Stick, a handbook on 3D printing with your new machine, and a bag of Gummy Bears. The USB stick contains several models, while PrusaSlicer is available for free download from the website. We also received a Buddy Camera and several boxes of filament to perform the review. Design of the Prusa CORE One+ INDX (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The CORE One+ INDX is a Core XY 3D printer converted into a toolchanger. It has a slim, steel exoskeleton with indents on either side. The right side holds a 3D-printed waste container on the outside for the tiny bits of filament the machine drops from the wiper system inside the chamber. We’re unsure if this mod is a permanent feature or an apology bonus for being unable to deliver fully hardened steel nozzles at launch. Like the original CORE One, the door and upper parts of the side panels are translucent black polymer. The top panel is now replaced by a “top hat” to give the multitude of Bowden tubes room to work. Since the shell is made of folded steel, it’s not exactly airtight, but so far we haven’t had any trouble printing ASA or ABS in the machine. The exoskeleton is an interesting concept. It provides a strong, stiff frame for the printer while also minimizing materials and avoiding that cheap plastic feel that plagues many other designs. The indented sides do more than slim down the printer’s silhouette; they reduce the interior space of the printer, allowing the chamber to be sufficiently heated (when needed) by only the heater bed. Like every other Prusa printer before it, several of the CORE One+ parts are 3D printed with PC Blend Carbon Fiber, though more pieces are moving to in-house injection molding. Most of the machine is manufactured at the main factory in Prague, though printers assembled in the United States will have some parts printed locally in Delaware. The CORE One+ has a door that can be flipped to open on either side. And thankfully, that door can remain closed at all times thanks to an active cooling system and automatic top vent. The INDX ditches the Nextruder extruder for the Bondtech induction-heated toolhead. The toolhead looks way too exposed out of necessity, as it picks up the passive nozzles by simply ramming itself onto the rack and grabbing the toolhead with magnets. The motion system is extremely accurate, and I had no problems with it during testing. You can see the copper coils of the induction heating system very plainly. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Unlike the Prusa XL, the toolheads mount on a rack in the front of the chamber. They take up very little space, but you will lose 15 mm of Y and 2 mm of X on the build plate compared to the CORE One+. The rack does make seeing inside the printer a bit of a challenge, but the optional Buddy Cam has a clear view from the inside. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The wiper is located to the side, on top of the indent. In the Founder’s Edition, the wiper dumped into a small removable cup clamped to the side panel. Our review unit has a hole drilled into it to dump into a large exterior container, which is a huge improvement. Image 1 of 3 (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Image 1 of 3 View Original Image 2 of 3 View Original Image 3 of 3 View Original Anyone who’s had to calibrate an XL will rejoice at the new automatic tool offset calibration system. A calibration sensor sits in the front corner of the machine, and you don’t need to do a thing but keep it clean. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The CORE One+ has active chamber temperature control, which is NOT the same as chamber heating. Instead, the machine’s interior geometry is optimized to capture heat thrown from the bed to heat the chamber up to 55C. A fan and smart ventilation system likewise keep the chamber cool enough for PLA even with the door closed. Assembling the Prusa CORE One+ INDX (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The Prusa CORE One+ INDX we reviewed came fully assembled and only needed to be unpacked. Simply pull it out of the box, remove the packing materials, snap the screen on and the spool holders, and plug it in. Once the machine is turned on, you’ll see a cartoon version of Josef Prusa to guide you through setup. However, calibration is now handled at the factory, so there’s nothing left to do but make sure you’ve removed the zip ties and carry on your merry way. Leveling the Prusa CORE One+ INDX (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Bed leveling is a no-brainer, as the Prusa CORE One+ is fully automatic. There are no manual adjustments and no need to adjust the Z offset. The printer uses a load cell sensor connected to the nozzle, which physically taps the print surface for precise measurement. The printer trams the bed and calculates the required Z height before each print. And yes, if you need it, live Z adjustments are available in the control panel. Loading Filament on the Prusa CORE One+ INDX (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Loading filament is very simple. Simply place the spools on the side-mounted rack and feed the plastic into the reverse Bowden tube until it reaches the hotend. You’ll need to open the printer menu and tell it which toolhead you’re loading, since the toolheads themselves are passive. The carriage will zip over, grab the requested tool, and take it to the nozzle wiper to purge a small amount of filament into the cup. It will wipe the nozzle and park the toolhead when you’re done. The inductive heater brings each nozzle up to temperature in a matter of seconds. Unfortunately, the printer only asks what kind of filament you’re loading (PLA, ASA, Flex, or more) but not what color. This is probably due to the fact that the slicer does not constantly communicate with the printer over the cloud, but I’m hoping that this feature will become available with a future firmware update. For now, you’ll have to manually enter your filament colors into the slicer. There is a remapping option on the control screen, but shifting around eight spools' worth of information in this fashion is tedious. The spoolholders are sturdy manual devices that can hold literally any brand of filament you might be using. They even expand to hold 3KG spools. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Preparing Files / Software for Prusa CORE One+ (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The Prusa CORE One+ uses its native slicer, PrusaSlicer. This open-source slicer is developed by Prusa Research and serves as the foundation for many other slicers. It comes with dozens of profiles for every material and nozzle size that Prusa Research makes. The slicer also has built- in Color Mixing, which allows you to blend two or three colors with ultra-fine layers to create the illusion of more colors. The CORE One+ can also use Prusa’s web-based slicer, EasyPrint, to print directly from Printables, Prusa’s free library of files, or from a mobile device. Printing on the Prusa CORE One+ INDX The fully assembled CORE One+ comes with a full 1 KG roll of Prusament PLA Galaxy Black. If you want more colors and materials like silks and multicolor filaments, you should check out our guide to the best filaments for 3D printing for suggestions. I used some of the sample rolls sent my way, plus a couple more lying about the workshop, to Prusa’s new calibration butterfly, Otto. This eight-color sample test print took 1 hour and 14 minutes. The wings are a first-layer test and are only two layers thick. A tab on the wing slots into the body to prove that tolerances and extrusion flow are correct. The multi-colored wing segments act as a visual test for first-layer quality, belt tension, and toolhead alignment, as any tiny offset in color boundaries or axis motion will show up instantly. This is a lot more useful than a Benchy for multicolor printing, and it makes a cool decoration you can keep on the shelf. Prusa Research, Otto the Calibration Butterfly (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) I printed this 100%, 150mm tall, Cinderwing3D Butterfly Dragon that I could never get to stick to the bed with other multicolor machines. Sitting next to it is a small container with all the waste this print produced from 1646 tool changes: 18 grams. When you look really close, they look like Nerds candy. This printed in 25 hours, 41 minutes, using a .2 mm layer

As Hungary undergoes an extensive policy remodeling after 16 years under the leadership of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, much focus has been on the new administration's efforts to uproot corruption, liberalize state institutions and rebuild ties with European allies. This effort by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who bested the longtime right-wing populist incumbent in an April election, has prompted a deluge of comparisons to a potential U.S. blueprint for a post-Trump era in the United States. But as Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán—no relation to the former prime minister—told Newsweek , pursuing close ties with Trump would be one of several areas spared from the new government's major overhaul. Read More on News "The relationship between the two countries is solid," Anita Orbán said during an interview on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. "The main alliance, which provides the framework, is, of course, NATO. So, the new Hungarian government aims to have an intensive, solid partnership with the U.S. administration." "We thankfully also inherited a couple of agreements or proposals or MOUs negotiated between the previous administration and the Trump administration," she added. "We are looking into all those, and we aim to progress with all those." ... 'We Are a Conservative Government' The comments came amid strained ties between Trump and a number of European countries which have been subject to frequent bouts of criticism from the White House. Since assuming office for a second non-consecutive term last January, Trump has accelerated rhetoric targeting trans-Atlantic allies with accusations of contributing too little on defense, maintaining unfair economic policies and pursuing harmful stances on immigration and other social issues. Until earlier this year, Viktor Orbán stood as an outlier who largely aligned with Trump's worldview. The former prime minister and his administration regularly charged the European Union with seeking a globalist, federalist agenda that would undermine Hungary's sovereignty and argued that European NATO members were prolonging the war in Ukraine launched by Russia, with which the former Hungarian administration cultivated strong ties. The Trump administration openly threw its weight behind Viktor Orbán's re-election, with Vice President JD Vance traveling to Budapest to support his campaign days before the vote. After the outcome, Trump said he "wasn’t that involved" in the effort to keep his ally in office, though he referred to Viktor Orbán as "a good man." Trump used the same description for Magyar, telling reporters at the time that "I think ​the new man's going to do a ⁠good job — he's a good man." Now, Anita Orbán said there was reason to believe the two countries would continue to find common ground as "we aim to have the same institutional, solid relationship" enjoyed under the previous administration. "In terms of values, we are aligned in quite many things," Anita Orbán said. "We are a conservative government, very much pro-faith. We are very strong on protecting children and families." Another key area she highlighted was the ongoing effort to tackle illegal migration, one of Viktor Orbán's strongest areas of alignment with Trump. "We will be strongly defending all borders and fences," Anita Orbán added. "So, the mandate of the electorate that the Tisza government received is overwhelming, it's resounding, but we need to be very clear where the mandate is continuity and where the mandate is change, even 180 degrees change." ... 'Defending Our National Interests' The Magyar administration's efforts to strike the right balance on its transformation of Hungarian politics also intersects with a sensitive debate on the degree to which the EU and other institutions would exert influence within the Central European nation being welcomed back into the fold. Anita Orbán said the strategy of rebuilding partnerships would not preclude voicing concerns when necessary. "We are going to represent the national interest of Hungary toward every country and national interest how we define it, what is good for Hungary's security, stability for the Hungarian people, for the Hungarians companies," Anita Orbán explained. "And what we saw is that the previous Hungarian administration was pulling out from the natural alliances Hungary belongs to, and that's EU and NATO." "And one of the flagship things that we announced is that we want to return to our alliances, which is EU and NATO as a trusted, constructive partner, which does not mean that we are not defending our national interests," she added. "It does not mean that we're not speaking up." She argued that the issue of sovereignty had been misrepresented under the previous government, used to justify dealings with foreign entities that did not represent Hungarian interests and promote influence campaigns to bring like-minded parties to power in other European countries. Under the new administration, Anita Orbán said the focus would be on promoting domestic initiatives, including economic rejuvenation, improved access to education, better healthcare programs and other areas. Fulfilling such promises, she said, could also provide momentum to mainstream parties under fire elsewhere in Europe, where movements more closely aligned with agendas promoted by Trump and Viktor Orbán are gaining substantial ground. "We had quite many years of experience with illiberal democracy and the experience of the Hungarian electorate was that there were words, words, and there was no delivery," Anita Orbán said. She attributed Magyar's electoral success in his ability to channel grassroots issues, speak plainly and avoid his rival's tendency to constantly frame his rhetoric around a fight with an "external enemy." "If we are successful, that can be for anybody," Anita Orbán said. "Anybody can vote right, left, mainstream, but anybody who would like to vote mainstream is looking now at the Hungarian story that we are really successful in creating, and bringing the country back in terms of an economic growth, in terms of a societal growth, and in terms of a stable foreign policy." ... 'A Lot of Experience' in Hybrid Warfare And yet, as Europe contends with a wave of internal political shifts trending away from mainstream parties, leaders are increasingly pointing to an outside threat, one posed by Russian President Vladimir Putin. Tensions related to the Russia-Ukraine war are spilling over into NATO territory , with a number of European officials warning of a potential major escalation from Moscow amid a growing number of drone sightings and other suspicious incidents. Trump has largely downplayed the concerns since a surprise visit by CIA chief John Ratcliffe to Moscow last month fanned further speculation over a looming Russian test of NATO's resolve. That the U.S. leader has repeatedly teased a withdrawal from NATO has only exacerbated European anxieties. But Anita Orbán did not share these worries. Rather, she read Trump's comments as a means of pushing European allies to contribute more on security, a principal with which she agreed, noting Hungary has already exceeded the 2 percent defense budget baseline for NATO members. " I would say that we need to adjust to the new realities and hear what the U.S. is saying and one of the consequences of this is really the burden shifting that European countries need to take a bigger stake in defending their own territory," Anita Orbán said. "It's not a concern at all that U.S. could withdraw." But whereas the previous government largely avoided direct criticism of the Kremlin, the Magyar administration has repeatedly spoken out, an approach Anita Orbán described as fundamental to upholding the alliance's unity, strength and capacity for deterrence. "We fully respect, of course, the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders and we do find the Russian activities alarming toward Europe," Anita Orbán said. This extends to "hybrid" warfare as well, in which she said Hungary had garnered "a lot of experience just from the campaign of interference" of pro-Viktor Orbán campaigns that Magyar has attributed to Moscow. Now, she asserted, "we do need to make sure that we are protecting our societies, protecting also the societies against disinformation and misinformation which has been widespread also in Hungary and protecting our borders." At the same time, even after Hungary expelled 10 Russian diplomats earlier this month, she emphasized that "the diplomatic channel has to be open, and it is open" with Russia despite most other European powers aiming to isolate the Kremlin. "Russia remains a supplier of energy to Hungary and remains an important regional player," Anita Orbán said. "So, of course, diplomatic channels have to be open." https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Andy Burnham has said that it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum. Photograph: Tuomas A Lehtinen/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham has said that it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum. Photograph: Tuomas A Lehtinen/Getty Images Brexit Letters We need to stop disinformation in UK political adverts. Here’s a chance to do so Alex Tait on a proposed amendment to the representation of the people bill, and Dr Joseph Mullen on Russian interference in the Brexit referendum Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.17 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.19 EDT Share Andy Burnham’s comments about Russian interference in Brexit ( Report, 11 October ) and the warning by the MI5 chief, Ken McCallum, against exaggerating its impact ( Report, 13 October ) risk overlooking another serious threat to electoral integrity: disinformation from our own political parties and campaigners. Foreign interference deserves scrutiny, but misleading factual claims in electoral advertising are unregulated, unlike in commercial advertising. We have four sets of rules to ensure an advert for a packet of sausages is accurate, but none for the most important advertising of all – ads that influence how we vote. With our fragmented five-party politics producing increasingly close elections, misleading advertising can be decisive. Brexit was decided by a 51.9%-48.1% vote split. Our research into May’s local elections found that 41.4% of wards in England were won by margins of less than 5%, with nine decided by a single vote. We also identified misleading electoral advertising in some of the closest contests. Regulating factual claims in electoral advertising was a key recommendation of the House of Lords select committee on democracy and digital technologies in 2020. The representation of the people bill , currently going through parliament, offers an opportunity to act. An amendment covering the same scope attracted 37 MPs as sponsors in the Commons, and we are working with peers in the Lords to take it forward. Burnham signed up to our voluntary code for honest electoral advertising in 2024, which forms part of the proposed amendments. We should tackle foreign interference, but we can’t continue to ignore the disinformation put out by our own political parties. Alex Tait Reform Political Advertising The head of MI5 confirming that Russia did try to interfere in the Brexit referendum is highly significant to the result. The vote share achieved by the leave campaign was 51.9%, as against 48.1% for the remainers. This was a majority of just 3.8%. If Russian interference swayed just 2% of voting intentions, this would erode the much-vaunted majority of the leave group, and remainers would emerge as victors. MI5 should carry out an impact assessment of Russian interference using the most up-to-date AI, and attempt to quantify shifts in voting patterns. This would go a long way towards introducing a new referendum. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck20.text: Image source, Handout Image caption, Brian Stack was shot in the back of the neck as he left a boxing match in 1983 By Gabija Gataveckaite ,Â Dublin correspondent, BBC News NI Â and Â Fiona Murray ,Â BBC News NI Published 21 October 2026, 06:21 BST Updated 4 hours ago The family of a senior Irish prison officer murdered by the IRA has received a state apology on Wednesday for failings in investigations into his killing. Brian Stack, a father of three, was crossing a street in Dublin, after leaving a boxing match in 1983, when he was shot in the back of the neck. Stack, who was the chief prison officer at the high-security Portlaoise Prison, was left paralysed and died 18 months later, aged 49. There were three separate garda (Irish police) investigations into Stack's death, but no-one was brought to justice for his killing. The Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) MicheÃ¡l Martin offered an apology on behalf of the state during a sitting of the DÃ¡il (Irish parliament). Stack's wife Sheila and her sons Austin, Kieran and Oliver were in the chamber for the apology. Martin said the Provisional IRA is "still in the possession of all the facts" on this case. 'Address our concerns, Sinn FÃ©in' The Stack brothers left the DÃ¡il (lower house of Irish parliament) chamber when Sinn FÃ©in TDs spoke during the State apology. Speaking outside Leinster House after the State apology, Austin Stack called on Sinn FÃ©in leader Mary Lou McDonald to "address our concerns" around their father's murder. "The IRA were responsible for the murder my father. The leader of the opposition has consistently said that the IRA campaign was justified," he said. "The leader of the opposition did not dignify and respect my family by coming into the chamber today and because of that, we took the action that we did, in withdrawing from the chamber when Sinn FÃ©in representatives were speaking." Image caption, The Stack family spoke outside Leinster House on Wednesday afternoon Speaking to reporters in Belfast, where she was being interviewed by the Police Service of Northern Ireland in relation to protests at Garvaghy Road , McDonald welcomed the State apology. "I can only imagine the trauma that they have been through for a long time," she said. "The IRA has acknowledged responsibility and expressed sorrow for the death of Brian Stack, has said that it shouldn't have happened and I think they made those statements very clearly more than a decade ago and I think that was the right and the correct thing to do." In a further statement, a Sinn FÃ©in spokesperson said a number of senior party TDs made contributions in the DÃ¡il, and that it was regrettable that McDonald was unable to attend due to her scheduled police interview. "Our thoughts are with Sheila Stack and her sons. Brian Stack's killing was wrong and should never have happened. We are deeply sorry for their loss and suffering. "Sinn FÃ©in acknowledges the hurt caused by republican actions in the past. We welcome the Irish government's apology for the investigative failures that compounded the family's pain. They deserve truth and justice. "Our position is clear: Investigating Brian Stack's killing is the responsibility of An Garda SÃ­ochÃ¡na. We support that work and the family's right to answers." Apology means 'an awful lot' Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme Brian Stack's son, Austin Stack, said the apology "means an awful lot to us". "It's a great sense of comfort, to particularly my mother and to myself and my two brothers, because the state is officially owning up to the errors and the omissions that happened," he said. He went on to say that the serious crime review team looked into the first investigation and "they found 194 errors and omissions". "So I have, and my family have, met with several ministers for justice down through the years and we have a requested sight of that report. "And every time we've requested it, we've been told that it's an internally valid document and that we cannot see it." Austin Stack said that Wednesday would be a very emotional day for his family. "My dad was doing a very difficult job at a very difficult time in our history," he said. "He was awarded the Irish Prison Service's highest bravery award for that work that he was doing. And this is further vindication of him and his good name." Prior to the DÃ¡il proceedings, the Stack family held a private meeting at government buildings with the taoiseach and Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan. 'Utterly unacceptable' Image source, PA Media Image caption, Taoiseach MicheÃ¡l Martin formally apologised to the Stack family In 2007 the Garda Commissioner directed a review of the case by the Garda Serious Crime Review Team. Over 200 recommendations were made relating to the cases. This review led to "serious failings" being found as well as "the shortcomings in the management" of the earlier Garda investigation. These failures, listed by Martin in the DÃ¡il, are: failure to keep a map made of the crime scene, a failure to keep a motorbike helmet found near the crime scene and linked to the crime, a failure to keep custody of material exhibits, including various fingerprints, samples and debris gathered during the investigation. The taoiseach also said there was a failure to document some potentially important aspects of the original investigation, including whether Brian's colleagues at Portlaoise Prison were interviewed and whether prisoners at the prison were interviewed. There was also a failure to interview the Stack family and to interview Brian's wider group of friends. "It is plainly and utterly unacceptable that material that was potentially of evidential value to the investigation can no longer be located by An Garda SÃ­ochÃ¡na. "It is admitted by An Garda SÃ­ochÃ¡na that these are serious matters that had an impact on the investigation," Martin said. He formally apologised to the Stack family for these failings. Image source, PA Media Image caption, NI secretary Sir Chris Bryant was asked about the matter in the House of Commons Speaking in the Commons during Northern Ireland questions on Wednesday, Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said he "warmly welcomed" the apology. Asked about the matter by Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson, Sir Chris said Dublin doing so was "entirely right and proper" and went to the heart of discussions MPs had been having this week as they debated the UK government's Troubles legacy bill . He added that it was "incumbent on all of us to make fulsome and not mealy-mouthed apologies". 'Regret' The IRA admitted killing Stack in 2013 after his family mounted a long campaign to secure the admission, and met Sinn FÃ©in's Gerry Adams and a former IRA commander. Adams, at that time, expressed his "regret" to the Stack family over the killing. A Sinn FÃ©in spokesperson said that "in a 2013 statement, a former IRA leader acknowledged that IRA volunteers were responsible for Brian Stack's killing". "The statement said the shooting had not been authorised by the IRA leadership, accepted IRA responsibility for his death, said it should not have happened and expressed sorrow for the pain and hurt suffered by the family." The spokesperson added: "As republicans, we acknowledge the hurt caused by republican actions. That suffering cannot be disowned. We are sorry for all the lives lost during the period of conflict on this island, without exception." Image source, PA Media Image caption, Irish foreign affairs minister Helen McEntee said the Provisional IRA "are responsible" Irish foreign affairs minister Helen McEntee also spoke during the State apology, she said: "The State failed you during their investigation into Brian's killing." She said Brian was "targeted" by the Provisional IRA and said "they are responsible". "To Sheila and to all of the Stack family, we are deeply sorry for all that you have endured, for the failures of the investigation and the additional suffering they have caused you, we are deeply sorry. I hope today's formal apology brings some measure of peace and comfort." Donegal Sinn FÃ©in TD (member of Irish parliament) Pearse Doherty said the Stack's family "long search for answers deserves respect". "No apology can restore Brian Stack's life or return the years spent seeking answers but it can recognise the wrong done." He said the failures of the garda investigation "compounded" the suffering of the Stack family. In 2019, the family received an apology from then garda commissioner Drew Harris in relation to the handling of the investigation into the murder. In 2023, gardaÃ­ told the family that the file on the case - which was with the DPP (Director of Public Prosecutions) - was being sent back to police for further investigation. Stack was the only prisoner officer in the state killed by violence related to the Troubles in Northern Ireland.
